html:
The Battle of Rocroi was fought on 19 May 1643 outside the fortress town of Rocroi in the Ardennes, in northeastern France. A French army under the 21-year-old Duke of Enghien, later called the Great Condé, beat a Spanish army under Francisco de Melo.

France had joined the Thirty Years' War against Spain and the emperor in 1635. In 1643 Melo invaded from the Spanish Netherlands and besieged Rocroi, on a road to Paris. King Louis XIII died on 14 May, leaving the crown to the four-year-old Louis XIV. Each side had about 23,000 men. The French left wing was driven back. But Enghien, on the right, broke the cavalry in front of him, then led his horsemen around behind the Spanish army and scattered the cavalry on the other wing as well. The Spanish infantry, the famous tercios, were left alone in the middle. They beat off several attacks. Most were killed or taken.

Spain could not easily replace these veteran soldiers. Its infantry had been thought almost unbeatable since Cerignola, and Rocroi ended that belief. Spain's decline was slower than the legend claims, but from this time France, not Spain, was the leading land power in Europe.
